title: The teacher
hook: a flower held up, a smile, and nothing said: Zen stresses face-to-face teaching

segments.voice: Yesterday: samu, the work period, and an old cook in the sun. Your line was work is practice. Which chore got the old cook's answer? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

Zen tells a story about a sermon with no words in it. The Buddha stands before a gathering of his followers, and instead of speaking, he lifts a single flower and turns it in his fingers. Nobody knows what to make of it. Except one disciple, Mahakashyapa, who smiles. And the Buddha, the story says, declares that something has passed to him, something the words of a sermon couldn't hold. A flower, a smile, and the beginning of a lineage. Today is about the person on the other side of the flower.
screen: `A FLOWER, HELD UP.` → `ONE DISCIPLE SMILES.` → `SOMETHING PASSES, WITHOUT WORDS.`

segments.voice: Zen puts a great deal of weight on the teacher, and on meeting face to face. First, the flower. The story is told as a case in The Gateless Gate, the same collection that opens with Zhaozhou's mu. Zen tells it as its own origin story, and its point is the picture: understanding passing between two people, directly. Second, the old verse. Tradition attributes to Bodhidharma, the teacher said to have carried Zen to China, a short description of the school, in paraphrase: a special transmission outside the scriptures, not depending on words and letters, pointing straight at the mind. Third, the catch. That doesn't mean Zen is against books. This whole week has leaned on Zen books: Dogen's writings, The Gateless Gate, Hakuin, Suzuki's talks. The point is that books aren't enough. A book can't see you. It can't tell when your answer to a koan is clever and when it's real. That's the teacher's job, and it happens in the private meeting we met earlier this week, where a student brings a response and a teacher looks back. Fourth, the line of people. Zen schools keep lineages: chains of teachers and students, each one taught by someone who was taught by someone. Tradition says Dogen crossed the sea to China in search of a teacher; that journey is how he met that old cook. The question this leaves for the rest of us is plain. Who, in your actual life, has taught you something face to face that you couldn't have gotten from a page?
screen: `A FLOWER AND A SMILE.` · `OUTSIDE THE SCRIPTURES, NOT IN WORDS.` · `A BOOK CAN'T SEE YOU.` · `A LINE OF TEACHERS, PERSON TO PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think who teaches you. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one person who taught you something in person. A grandparent at a stove. A coach. A boss who showed you how, not just told you. A friend who said the hard thing to your face. Let their face come clear. What did they pass on that you couldn't have read? If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If not, just sit with them a moment, face to face in memory. The bell holds the time.
The teacher. In Zen, the person who meets you face to face, and passes on what words alone can't carry. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. Today, thank one of your teachers, in person or by voice if you can, and tell them one thing you still carry from them. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Zen students usually practice under a teacher, meeting in private interviews to bring questions and koan responses, and Zen schools trace their teachers in lineages.

fork.setup: the Buddha stands before a crowd and, without a word, holds up a flower. what does Mahakashyapa do?
fork.reveal: he smiles, and the story says something passes to him that a sermon's words couldn't hold.

original.note: Japanese: mind to mind, a phrase Zen uses for teaching that passes directly between teacher and student.

trapdoor: what you thought: Zen says skip the books and just meditate.
what it means: Zen leans on a living teacher, face to face, because a book can't see you.
what a scholar hears: the flower story as Zen's own origin tale, the verse tradition credits to Bodhidharma, and lineages of teachers, person to person.
